description: The system-design ideas big companies expect from junior to mid-level engineers: estimation, scaling, load balancing, caching, databases, replication, sharding, consistency, messaging, idempotency, sagas and the outbox, plus classic designs. CAP is stated precisely: during a network partition you trade consistency against availability.

cards.front: How should you start a system-design answer before drawing boxes?
cards.back: Clarify who uses it, the read and write rates, the latency target, the data size, and what must not be wrong. Then estimate, then draw.
cards.explanation: A news feed and a payments ledger do not share a design. Ask: strong consistency or is slightly stale data fine? How many requests per second? How large is one object? Back-of-the-envelope math (QPS times payload times seconds in a day) tells you whether one database is enough. Mid-level candidates fail by jumping to Kafka. Junior candidates fail by drawing one box labeled 'server'. Spend the first few minutes on constraints.
cards.example: 10 million daily active users, each loading a feed 20 times a day, is about 200 million reads a day, roughly 2,300 reads per second on average, with a peak several times that.

cards.front: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
cards.back: Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and requires the work to be shareable.
cards.explanation: Vertical scaling is simple until you hit the largest box you can buy, and that box is still a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling needs a way to spread requests, shared-nothing app servers, and a plan for state. Sessions stored in one server's memory break horizontal scaling. Put session state in a shared store or in a signed cookie. Databases are harder to scale horizontally than stateless app servers.
cards.example: A payments API with no in-memory session can sit behind a load balancer on ten identical instances.

cards.front: What does a load balancer decide, and what is the L4 versus L7 distinction?
cards.back: It spreads connections across healthy instances and stops sending traffic to dead ones. L4 balances using IP and port. L7 understands HTTP and can route by path or header.
cards.explanation: Health checks must hit a real dependency or you will send users to a process that is up but cannot reach its database. Least-connections helps when requests vary in cost. Round-robin is enough when they do not. Sticky sessions hide a state bug. Prefer not to need them. An L7 balancer can send /api/search to a different pool than /api/checkout.
cards.example: If the health check only opens a TCP port, a deadlocked JVM still receives traffic.

cards.front: Explain cache-aside, and name two ways it fails in production.
cards.back: The application reads the cache first. On a miss it reads the database and writes the cache. Failures: stampedes on a popular miss, and serving stale data after a write if you forget to invalidate.
cards.explanation: A cache is a latency optimization, not the source of truth, unless you deliberately design a write-through or write-back cache. Set a TTL so a missed invalidation heals. A stampede happens when a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database together. Mitigations: lock a single refresher, or serve slightly stale data while one request refreshes (single-flight). Cache the hot path only. Caching everything wastes memory and makes invalidation unknowable.
cards.example: On update of product 42, delete cache key product:42 or overwrite it in the same flow as the database write.

cards.front: What is a database index, and what do you pay for it?
cards.back: An index is a side structure, usually a B-tree, that maps a key to row locations so a lookup is O(log n) pages instead of a full scan. Every insert and update must maintain it.
cards.explanation: Indexes speed reads and slow writes. A column with low selectivity, such as a boolean, often does not deserve its own index. Composite index order matters: an index on (user_id, created_at) serves 'this user, newest first', not 'all rows from yesterday' efficiently. The query planner may ignore an index if it expects to read most of the table. Look at the actual plan. Do not add indexes by folklore.
cards.example: WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 wants a composite index starting with user_id.

cards.front: When do you pick a relational database, and when do you pick a key-value or document store?
cards.back: Relational when you need transactions, constraints, and flexible queries across related rows. Key-value when you only fetch by a known key and need very low latency. Document when each record's shape varies and you load it as a unit.
cards.explanation: Joins and multi-row transactions are the relational database's job. Spreading those across services without a transaction is a new failure mode, not a free performance win. Wide-column stores such as Cassandra fit huge write volumes addressed by a row key, for example time-series events. 'NoSQL scales' is incomplete. It scales a particular access pattern. Name the query before you name the product.
cards.example: A shopping cart keyed by user id can be a key-value record. An order with payments, refunds, and line items wants relational constraints.

cards.front: What is replication, and what lag does a follower add?
cards.back: Replication copies data to another node so you can survive a failure and spread reads. Asynchronous followers can be behind the leader, so a read-after-write may miss the write.
cards.explanation: Synchronous replication is safer and slower: the write does not succeed until another node has it. Asynchronous replication loses the last writes if the leader dies before shipping them. A common bug is writing to the leader and immediately reading from a replica. Fixes: read-your-writes routing to the leader for that user, or a version check. Replication is not a backup. A bad UPDATE replicates too.
cards.example: User saves a profile, the next GET hits a replica that has not applied the update, and the UI looks like the save failed.

cards.front: What is sharding, and what makes a shard key dangerous?
cards.back: Sharding splits rows across databases by a key, so no single machine holds every row. A bad key sends most traffic to one shard.
cards.explanation: user_id is often a good key because one user's data stays together and load spreads. A timestamp key puts today's writes on one shard. Resharding is an operational project, so pick a key you can live with. Cross-shard transactions and joins become application code. If the data fits on one primary plus replicas, do not shard yet. Mid-level judgment is knowing when not to.
cards.example: Hashing a monotonically increasing order id into 16 shards spreads inserts. Sharding by country can put most users on one shard.

cards.front: Why does hash(key) % N fall apart when you add a cache node?
cards.back: Almost every key changes bucket when N changes, so the cache misses all at once and the database gets a stampede.
cards.explanation: Consistent hashing places nodes on a ring. A key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node takes only the keys that fall in its new arc, about 1/N of them, not all of them. Virtual nodes (many points per machine) stop one server from owning a huge empty arc. This is how caches, Cassandra, and similar systems add capacity. It does not by itself fix a hot key. A celebrity user still hits one node. Replicate or salt that key.
cards.example: With N = 4, key 10 maps to 10 % 4 = 2. With N = 5 it maps to 0. Those are different servers, and the same happens for most keys.

cards.front: What does the CAP theorem actually force you to choose?
cards.back: When a network partition splits nodes, a distributed store cannot be both fully consistent and fully available. It must pick which one to give up until the partition heals.
cards.explanation: The slogan 'pick any two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance' is the interview shorthand and it misleads. Real networks do partition, so tolerance is not optional. During the partition: a CP system refuses some requests rather than serve stale or divergent data. An AP system answers and repairs later (eventual consistency). Consistency here means a strong, linearizable read, not 'the code is correct'. Many systems are neither pure CP nor pure AP. They choose per operation.
cards.example: A bank ledger may reject a withdrawal it cannot confirm (CP). A hit counter on a video may increment on whichever node you reached and reconcile later (AP).

cards.front: What is eventual consistency, in one precise sentence?
cards.back: If writes stop, all replicas eventually return the same value. Until then, reads may disagree.
cards.explanation: It is not 'the system is inconsistent forever'. It is a convergence promise. Users feel it as a like-count that jumps backward, or a photo that is missing for a few seconds after upload. If the product cannot tolerate that, do not put that operation on an eventually consistent path. Conflict resolution (last write wins, or a merge function) has to be chosen or you will drop updates silently.
cards.example: Two editors change a document offline. Last-write-wins keeps one edit and destroys the other. A merge keeps both if the data allows it.

cards.front: Why put a message queue between two services?
cards.back: So a slow or down consumer does not fail the producer. The queue absorbs bursts, and consumers pull at their own pace.
cards.explanation: You trade immediate consistency for decoupling. The producer must not assume the consumer has finished. Deliveries are often at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent: processing the same message twice cannot double-charge. Ordering is usually per partition key, not global. A queue does not replace a database. Messages are not a system of record unless you design for that and accept the operational cost.
cards.example: Checkout writes the order, then publishes OrderPlaced. Email and warehouse consume it. If email is down, checkout still succeeds and the message waits.

cards.front: What is the difference between at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery?
cards.back: At-most-once may drop a message and does not retry. At-least-once retries and may deliver duplicates. Exactly-once is usually 'effectively once' via idempotent processing plus deduplication, not a magical network.
cards.explanation: Networks cannot promise exactly-once by themselves: the receiver may process the message and the acknowledgement may be lost, so the sender retries. The practical design is at-least-once delivery and an idempotency key stored with the side effect. Mid-level engineers who say 'we'll use exactly-once Kafka' without mentioning the consumer transaction are hand-waving.
cards.example: A payment message carries a unique charge id. The consumer inserts that id in a unique column. The second delivery hits the constraint and does not charge again.

cards.front: How does a token-bucket rate limiter work?
cards.back: The bucket holds tokens and refills at a steady rate up to a maximum. Each request takes a token. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected or delayed.
cards.explanation: The burst size is the bucket capacity. The sustained rate is the refill. This allows a short spike, which a fixed window counter handles badly (two bursts at the edges of adjacent windows). For many API servers, store the bucket in Redis so the limit is global, not per process. Return 429 and a Retry-After header. Rate limiting protects you. It does not replace authentication.
cards.example: Capacity 50, refill 10 tokens per second: a client may send 50 at once, then about 10 per second.

cards.front: What is a single point of failure, and what is the cheapest way to remove one?
cards.back: A component whose death takes the product down. The cheapest fix is a second instance plus a health-checked load balancer, or a replica that can be promoted.
cards.explanation: Two instances in the same availability zone still die together if the zone dies. Spread them. A single database primary is often the remaining SPOF after the app tier is redundant. Backups do not help a failure you must survive in seconds. They help a failure you can restore from. Say the recovery time you are designing for. Mid-level answers include that number.
cards.example: One NAT gateway, one cache node with no replica, or one cron host that nobody monitors.

cards.front: What does a circuit breaker stop?
cards.back: It stops calling a dependency that is already failing, so your threads do not all block on it. After a cooldown it lets a few trial calls through.
cards.explanation: States are closed (normal), open (fail fast), and half-open (probe). Without it, a slow payments service occupies every request thread and your API dies too — a cascading failure. Timeouts are required even with a breaker. A breaker without a timeout still waits. Fallbacks must be honest: a cached price is fine, inventing a successful payment is not.
cards.example: If 50% of inventory calls fail in 10 seconds, open the breaker and return 'unavailable' for 30 seconds instead of piling up waits.

cards.front: Why is OFFSET pagination a problem on a large table, and what replaces it?
cards.back: OFFSET 100000 still makes the database walk and discard 100000 rows. Cursor pagination asks for 'rows after this last seen key' and uses an index.
cards.explanation: OFFSET pages also shift if new rows are inserted: the user sees duplicates or skips. A cursor is the last (created_at, id) pair, and the next query is WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. It needs a matching index. Cursors are worse for 'jump to page 500'. That feature is rarely worth the cost.
cards.example: SELECT ... FROM events WHERE id < :cursor ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;

cards.front: What does a CDN do, and what should you not put behind it blindly?
cards.back: A CDN caches bytes at edge locations near users so static content does not travel to your origin every time. Do not cache personalized or authorized responses unless the cache key includes the user and you meant to.
cards.explanation: Cache-Control headers decide what the edge may store. A missing Vary or a shared cache of a response that contains a private cookie is a data leak. Invalidate or version asset URLs when you deploy, or clients keep yesterday's JavaScript. The origin must still survive a cache flush, because a flush is a thundering herd.
cards.example: Image and JS URLs are cached for a year and include a content hash. The HTML that points at them is cached for a minute.

cards.front: A query is slow. What do you check, in order, before you add a cache?
cards.back: The actual query plan, whether an index matches the filter and the order, how many rows you fetch, and whether you have an N+1 query loop.
cards.explanation: A cache in front of a full table scan hides the cost until the cache misses, then the database falls over. N+1 means one query for a page of orders and one query per order for its items. Batch them or join them. Measure. A mid-level engineer names the evidence: rows examined, index used, p95 latency. Only then add a cache for a read that is hot and expensive.
cards.example: Loading 20 orders should not issue 21 queries. One query for orders and one WHERE order_id IN (...) for items is enough.

cards.front: How do you talk about tradeoffs without freezing in an interview?
cards.back: State the choice, what it optimizes, what it makes worse, and which constraint in this problem makes the choice acceptable.
cards.explanation: Example shape: 'I will shard by user_id so a user's reads stay on one shard. Cross-user search becomes a fan-out, which we said is rare. If search were the main feature I would not shard this way.' That sentence is worth more than a diagram of every technology you know. Junior answers list tools. Mid-level answers defend a decision.
cards.example: Cache-aside lowers read latency and adds staleness up to the TTL. The product said a 30-second delay on the feed is fine, so the TTL is 30 seconds.

cards.front: How do you turn 'X requests per day' into requests per second for a quick estimate?
cards.back: A day has 86,400 seconds, roughly 100,000. So 1 million requests per day is about 12 per second on average. Then multiply by a peak factor (often 2-10×) for the busiest hour.
cards.explanation: Back-of-the-envelope numbers decide whether you need one database or a sharded fleet. Also estimate storage: items per day × size × retention. Round aggressively and say your assumptions out loud.
cards.example: 10M daily users × 20 reads each = 200M reads/day ≈ 2,300/s average, maybe 10,000/s at peak. 1M new posts/day × 1 KB × 365 days ≈ 365 GB per year.

cards.front: Which latency numbers should every engineer know roughly?
cards.back: Main memory read: ~100 ns. SSD random read: ~100 µs. Round trip inside one datacenter: ~0.5 ms. Disk seek on spinning disk: ~10 ms. Round trip across continents: ~100-150 ms.
cards.explanation: The gaps are what matter: memory is about 1,000× faster than SSD, and a cross-region call costs about 300 in-datacenter round trips. That is why chatty service-to-service calls and cross-region synchronous calls hurt so much.
cards.example: An endpoint that makes 40 sequential calls to another service at 2 ms each spends 80 ms on network waits alone. Batch them or call in parallel.

cards.front: What is an idempotency key, and why do payment APIs require one?
cards.back: A unique client-generated ID sent with a non-idempotent request (like POST /payments). The server stores the key with the result and returns the same result for retries instead of charging again.
cards.explanation: Networks fail after the server processed a request but before the client got the response. The client must retry, and without a key the retry creates a duplicate. Store the key with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the side effect.
cards.example: POST /payments with header Idempotency-Key: 5f1c...; a retry with the same key returns the original 201 response.

cards.front: What is the dual-write problem, and how does the transactional outbox pattern fix it?
cards.back: Writing to the database and publishing to a message broker are two separate operations; if one fails, they disagree. With the outbox, you write the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction, and a separate relay publishes rows from that table to the broker.
cards.explanation: The relay may publish an event more than once, so consumers must be idempotent. Relays can poll the table or use change data capture (for example Debezium reading the database log).
cards.example: BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders ...; INSERT INTO outbox(type, payload) VALUES ('OrderPlaced', ...); COMMIT; then the relay sends to Kafka and marks the row sent.

cards.front: What is a saga, and why is it used instead of a distributed transaction (two-phase commit)?
cards.back: A saga splits a business transaction across services into local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. 2PC locks resources across services and blocks if the coordinator fails, so it is rarely used between microservices.
cards.explanation: Sagas give eventual consistency: there are intermediate states users might see (order 'pending'). Orchestration uses a central coordinator; choreography lets services react to each other's events. Compensations must be idempotent and can't always truly undo (an email already sent).
cards.example: Place order → reserve stock → charge card. If the charge fails: release stock, mark order cancelled.

cards.front: What is 'read-your-writes' consistency, and how do read replicas break it?
cards.back: A user should always see their own changes right after making them. With asynchronous replicas, a write goes to the primary but the next read may hit a replica that hasn't caught up, so the user's change seems to disappear.
cards.explanation: Fixes: read from the primary for a short time after a user's write, route that user's reads to the primary for their own data, or track the replication position and wait for the replica to reach it.
cards.example: User edits their profile name, page reloads from a replica 300 ms behind, and shows the old name.

cards.front: What does R + W > N mean in quorum-based replication?
cards.back: With N replicas, if a write must be acknowledged by W of them and a read queries R of them, then R + W > N guarantees at least one replica in every read has the latest acknowledged write.
cards.explanation: Common setting: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2. Lower W gives faster writes but weaker reads; tuning these trades latency against consistency. Used by Dynamo-style stores like Cassandra (consistency level QUORUM).
cards.example: N = 3, W = 1, R = 1: fast, but a read can miss a write that reached only one other node.

cards.front: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read for a news feed?
cards.back: Fan-out on write pushes each new post into every follower's precomputed feed (fast reads, expensive writes). Fan-out on read builds the feed at read time by pulling recent posts from followed accounts (cheap writes, slower reads).
cards.explanation: Real systems mix both: push for normal users, pull for celebrities with millions of followers, then merge at read time. This hybrid avoids writing one post into 50 million feeds.
cards.example: A user with 200 followers posts: push to 200 feed lists in Redis. A celebrity posts: store once; followers' feed reads merge it in.

cards.front: How do you design a URL shortener at a high level?
cards.back: Generate a short unique ID (base62 of a counter or a random ID with a collision check), store id → long URL in a key-value store, put a cache in front because reads dominate, and redirect with HTTP 301 or 302.
cards.explanation: 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, reducing load but hiding repeat clicks from analytics; 302 (temporary) sends every click to you. Sequential IDs are guessable; add randomness if links must not be enumerable. 7 base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion IDs.
cards.example: GET /aZ3kP9q → cache hit → 302 Location: https://example.com/very/long/path

cards.front: How do you generate unique IDs across many servers?
cards.back: Options: random UUIDv4 (no coordination, but random index inserts), time-ordered UUIDv7 (sortable, index-friendly), Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (timestamp + machine ID + sequence), or database sequences (simple but central).
cards.explanation: Random UUIDs as primary keys scatter writes across a B-tree index and hurt insert performance; time-ordered IDs append near the end. Snowflake IDs depend on synchronized clocks and unique machine IDs.
cards.example: Snowflake layout: 41 bits of milliseconds since an epoch, 10 bits of machine ID, 12 bits of per-millisecond sequence.

cards.front: How does Kafka order messages, and what limits consumer parallelism?
cards.back: Order is guaranteed only within a partition. Messages with the same key go to the same partition, so per-key order holds. Within a consumer group, each partition is read by one consumer, so active consumers ≤ number of partitions.
cards.explanation: Pick the key that needs ordering (orderId, accountId). Adding consumers beyond the partition count gives idle consumers. A hot key sends all its traffic to one partition and one consumer.
cards.example: Topic with 12 partitions keyed by accountId: up to 12 consumers in parallel, and each account's events are processed in order.

cards.front: What is backpressure, and what happens without it?
cards.back: A way for a slow consumer to tell a fast producer to slow down, by blocking, rejecting, or signaling capacity. Without it, queues and buffers grow until memory runs out or latency explodes.
cards.explanation: Bounded queues are the simplest form: when full, block the producer or reject with 429/503 so clients back off. Unbounded queues only hide overload until the process dies.
cards.example: ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and CallerRunsPolicy slows down the submitting thread when workers fall behind.

cards.front: Where should user-uploaded files go, and how do clients upload them?
cards.back: In object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), with only metadata and the object key in the database. Clients upload directly using a short-lived presigned URL, so file bytes don't pass through your service.
cards.explanation: Storing large blobs in a relational database bloats backups and replication. Serve downloads through a CDN or presigned GET URLs. Validate type and size, and scan if needed, after upload.
cards.example: POST /uploads → server returns presigned PUT URL valid for 10 minutes → browser PUTs the file to S3 → client confirms with the object key.

cards.front: Polling vs long polling vs Server-Sent Events vs WebSockets?
cards.back: Polling asks repeatedly on a timer. Long polling holds the request open until data arrives. SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream over HTTP. WebSockets are a full two-way persistent connection.
cards.explanation: SSE is simple and enough for notifications and live dashboards. WebSockets suit chat, collaboration, and games. Persistent connections make load balancing and deploys harder because connections must be drained and clients must reconnect.
cards.example: Build status page: SSE. Collaborative editor: WebSockets. Daily report status: plain polling every 30 s is fine.

cards.front: Microservices vs a modular monolith: how do you choose?
cards.back: A modular monolith is one deployable with strong internal module boundaries. Microservices are separately deployed services that own their data. Microservices buy independent deploys and scaling at the cost of network calls, distributed data, and much more operational work.
cards.explanation: Split when teams block each other on deploys, or parts need very different scaling or reliability, not because it's fashionable. A good rule: start with clear modules; extract a service when a boundary is proven and the pain is real.
cards.example: Five engineers, one product: modular monolith. 30 teams with separate domains and release cycles: services.

cards.front: How do you add full-text search to a system whose source of truth is a relational database?
cards.back: Index documents in a search engine (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) built on an inverted index (term → list of documents), and keep it in sync from the database via events or change data capture.
cards.explanation: The search index is a derived, eventually consistent copy; it can always be rebuilt from the source of truth. Simple cases can start with the database's own full-text search (PostgreSQL tsvector) before adding another system.
cards.example: Product updated in Postgres → Debezium emits a change event → indexer updates the Elasticsearch document within seconds.

cards.text: During a network partition, CAP says you trade {{c1::consistency}} against availability.
cards.extra: Partition tolerance is not optional on a real network. CP refuses some requests. AP answers and reconciles later. 'Pick any two' is the loose slogan.

cards.text: hash(key) % N moves most keys when {{c1::N}} changes. Consistent hashing does not.
cards.extra: On a ring, a new node takes only the keys in its arc. Virtual nodes smooth the imbalance. A single hot key still needs replication or salting.

cards.text: At-least-once delivery requires the consumer to be {{c1::idempotent}}.
cards.extra: A retry after a lost acknowledgement will run the side effect twice unless a unique key makes the second run a no-op.

cards.text: 1 million requests per day is about {{c1::12}} requests per second on average.
cards.extra: A day has 86,400 seconds. Remember to apply a peak factor.

cards.text: In Kafka, ordering is guaranteed only within a {{c1::partition}}, so messages that must stay ordered share the same {{c2::key}}.
cards.extra: Active consumers in a group can't exceed the number of partitions.

cards.text: The transactional {{c1::outbox}} pattern writes the event in the same database transaction as the business change.
cards.extra: A relay publishes it afterwards; consumers must be idempotent.
